sections.title: What microservices buy you — and cost you

blocks.text: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services, each owning a business capability and its data. The benefits are organisational as much as technical: teams ship independently, services scale independently, and failures can be isolated. The costs are distributed-systems costs: network calls instead of function calls, partial failures, eventual consistency, and much more operational surface area.

cols.title: Modular monolith
pros: One deploy, in-process calls, ACID across modules
cons: Scales as one unit; one bad deploy affects everything

cols.title: Microservices
pros: Independent deploys and scaling; fault isolation
cons: Network latency and failures; distributed data; heavy ops tooling

sections.title: The edge: API gateway and BFF

blocks.caption: Request path in a microservice architecture

items: The gateway handles cross-cutting concerns once: TLS, authentication, rate limits, request ids.
A **Backend-for-Frontend** composes several service calls into the exact shape a screen needs, so phones don't make 12 round trips.
Each service owns its database; others access the data only via its API or events.

blocks.text: In Kubernetes, a Service object gives a stable DNS name and virtual IP that load-balances across healthy pods; a service mesh adds smarter, per-request balancing.

items: **Sync (REST/gRPC)** when the caller needs the answer to continue ("is this payment authorised?"). Add timeouts, retries, circuit breakers.
**Async (events)** when the caller just needs to announce something happened ("OrderPlaced"). Consumers react independently; producers don't know or wait for them.
Avoid long synchronous chains: availability multiplies (five 99.9% services in series ≈ 99.5%) and latencies add.

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Prefer events for propagating state changes between services and synchronous calls only for queries that genuinely need a real-time answer.

A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) injects a sidecar proxy next to every service instance. The sidecars handle mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, traffic splitting for canaries and uniform telemetry, configured from a central control plane. It removes boilerplate from every codebase at the cost of extra hops (~1 ms), resource overhead and a complex control plane to operate.

items: **Database per service** — sharing tables couples deploys and schemas.
Cross-service consistency via **sagas** and the **transactional outbox**, not distributed transactions.
Queries that span services: build a read model (CQRS) fed by events, or compose in a BFF.
Reference data other services need: replicate it via events into local read-only copies.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: The distributed monolith: services that must be deployed together, share a database, or call each other synchronously in long chains. You pay the costs of microservices and get none of the benefits.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'd start with a few coarse services split by business capability, each owning its data, talking via events for state changes and gRPC for real-time queries, behind a gateway with per-client BFFs.
